Load path

Reads the "Export Load Path" pyRevit button's output — traces each column/wall down through the model's physical geometry (columns, walls, beams, footings) to the footing it lands on, flags any that don't connect all the way down, and estimates a rough gravity load per footing from a simple nearest-neighbor tributary area × each level's own dead/live load, set per level below. Not a substitute for a real structural analysis.

Checking for a load path export…
Everything here already recomputes as you type — this is here for a one-click refresh after changing several fields at once.

Level loads▾

Dead and live/snow load per level, read straight off your General Notes sheet — one row per level found in this project's export, roof levels called out separately. Applied per-member by its own level: a column's footing load sums each story's own DL+LL x tributary area, not one blanket number for the whole building. Used by the Footings table below (for both column point loads and, using the wall tributary width above, wall line loads on continuous footings) and the Beam / Joist Check. Values are remembered per project/level in this browser.

Broken / unresolved load paths▾

These columns or walls don't connect down to a footing within the search tolerance — could be a real modeling gap, or just this tool's endpoint-matching missing an unusual connection. Worth a visual check in Revit either way.

Isolated (bearing) footings▾

Column loads only — each connected column's own tributary load, summed per footing. Wall loads never contribute here.

Continuous footings▾

Wall loads only, per linear foot — column loads never contribute here. Which table a footing appears in is decided by the footing's own type/geometry (isolated pad vs. continuous strip), not by which load traced to it — foundation slabs are excluded entirely. A column load that traces to a continuous footing, or a wall load that traces to an isolated pad, is flagged in the summary above as a likely trace mismatch worth checking manually, rather than pulled into this table. Each wall's tributary width is computed from your actual modeled floors (not a single typed-in number) — the "Wall tributary width fallback" field above is only used where that couldn't be computed.

Beam / Joist Check▾

Flags modeled beams/joists that look undersized for their span, reusing the same bending/shear/deflection math as the LVL/I-Joist Calc tab. Tributary width here is a single value applied to every member (this project's typical joist/beam spacing) — not read per-member, so treat this as a first pass, not a per-beam design check. A member whose size couldn't be parsed from its family/type name is flagged rather than guessed. Open Web Wood Joists (OWWJ) are assumed to bear only at their two ends — they are never flagged as multi-span continuous, even if a column happens to sit under the middle of one.

Dead/live loads come from the Level loads table above — each beam/joist uses its own level's values. Tributary width is measured per-member from the modeled spacing to its nearest parallel neighbor on the same level (half-distance each side) — the fallback below is used only when no neighbor running alongside a member can be found.

3D view▾

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom. Green = column/wall with a resolved load path to a footing, red = broken/unresolved, gray boxes = footings. Blue-gray lines are beams, shown for context only — not traced further down this pass.

Snow Drift Key Plan

Open the roof plan sheet, set the snow criteria, and click along each roof step, parapet or rooftop unit to calculate its drift (ASCE 7-16 §7.7–7.8). Drifts draw live as a hatched band with the drift triangle and PSF tag. Save the drift file; in Revit, Import Snow Drifts places the bands, triangles and tags into the plan view on that sheet.

Drifts on this sheet

Add drift: click the two ends of the wall/parapet/step edge. The drift side is picked for you (the lower roof); use Drift on the other side in the dialog if it's wrong. Measure: click two points to read a length (it's pre-filled into the next drift). Values follow ASCE 7-16: hd = 0.43∛lu·∜(pg+10) − 1.5 (lu ≥ 20 ft), windward = 0.75hd, γ = 0.13pg+14 ≤ 30, w = 4hd (or 4hd²/hc ≤ 8hc when hd > hc), no drift when hc/hb < 0.2. Confirm against the engineer's own calculation.

Notes

All the caveats, assumptions, and code-basis notes from every tab, collected here. Each calculator links back to its own section with a "See Notes" link instead of carrying the full paragraph inline.

Issues, problems & suggestions

Found something wrong or have an idea? Log it here. Items are saved in the shared SE Review folder (Feedback/feedback.json), so everyone connected to that folder sees the same list.

Beam Sizing

Point loads above are optional and superposed onto whichever bay/overhang they fall in. Bending is checked two ways and the larger governs: (1) each bay as its own simple span and each overhang as a cantilever (M=w·a²/2 at the support), and (2) the whole beam as one continuous member over all supports, dead load everywhere and live load patterned span-by-span, enveloped — this is what captures negative moment over interior supports. Deflection is still checked per bay/overhang as simple span/cantilever (conservative). The shear/moment diagrams and support reactions come from the continuous analysis. Post vs. Wall is a label only in the diagram — it doesn't change this calculation; a wall (continuous) support in reality shares load differently than a discrete post, which matters for a real bearing/hanger design even though it doesn't change the beam's own bending/deflection check. Width is fixed by your selection above (or your custom entry) — the calculator solves only for the required depth at that width; it will not swap you to a different width to save material. Default is 5-1/2", Tamarack's typical beam width. Note two separate glulam width families exist: 5-1/2"/7-1/2"/9-1/2" are the Southern Pine series, manufactured net-width to match dimension lumber (flush with a 2x6/2x8/2x10 wall or post); 3-1/8"/5-1/8"/6-3/4"/8-3/4" are the Western species (Douglas Fir) series, which do NOT match dimension lumber widths. A custom width/Fb/E lets you check a sawn timber, LVL, PSL, or a glulam width/grade not in the lists above — Sx/I are still generated from simple rectangular geometry (b·d), so this isn't valid for a non-rectangular or built-up unequal-ply section. The species/grade picker for custom Fb just fills in typical dimension-lumber base values (No. 1/No. 2 unless noted) as a starting point — confirm the actual grade stamp and current NDS Supplement value for your specific size before specifying, since large-timber (beam & stringer) reference values differ from dimension-lumber values. Confirm which series your supplier stocks before specifying. Verify bearing, lateral-torsional buckling (CL), and connection design separately. Support reactions shown below the beam are continuous-beam reactions (max over live-load patterns) per this beam's own loads only — they don't include the beam's self-weight or anything stacking on top of that post elsewhere in the structure, so add those before sizing a footing.

Snow Loads (unbalanced / sliding / curved)

Common: pf = 0.7CeCtIspg, raised to the jurisdiction minimum if you enter one. γ = 0.13pg+14 ≤ 30 pcf. Drift height hd uses Fig. 7.6-1 with lu = W and the figure's 20 ft minimum. Cs is from Fig. 7.4-1 using the Ct and surface you pick (warm Ct ≤ 1.0, 1.1, or cold 1.2 curves). Gable unbalanced (§7.6.1): only required for pitches from 1/2:12 to 7:12. For W ≤ 20 ft with simple rafters spanning eave to ridge: windward 0, leeward Ispg uniform. Otherwise windward 0.3ps, leeward ps plus a rectangular surcharge hdγ/√S extending (8/3)hd√S from the ridge. Sliding (§7.9): 0.4pfW plf spread over 15 ft of lower roof (= 0.4pfW/15 psf on top of the lower roof's balanced load); if the lower roof is narrower than 15 ft the load is cut in proportion, so the psf stays the same over the shorter width. Only applies when the upper roof is steeper than 1/4:12 (slippery) or 2:12 (non-slippery). Not combined with a drift here — check that separately. Curved roofs (§7.6.2, Fig. 7.6-2): the roof is taken as a circular arc from span and rise. Unbalanced is skipped when the line from eave (or the 70° point) to crown is flatter than 10° or steeper than 60°. Windward side 0; leeward rises linearly from 0.5pf at the crown to 2pfCs/Ce at the eave (case 1, eave < 30°), or at the 30° point then to 2pfCs,eave/Ce at the eave (case 2, 30–70°), or at the 30° point then to zero at the 70° point (case 3, eave > 70°). Loads are interpolated at each panel point by horizontal distance from the crown.

LVL / I-Joist Calc

Assumes simple span, load at midspan for the point load, superposition of uniform + point load effects. Sawn lumber and LVL values are representative base design values (no CD/CM/CL/CF adjustment applied) — treat as a starting point, not a final design. I-joist depths are picked from generic representative capacities, not a specific product line.

Joist Spans

Calculated from standard NDS-style Fb/E design values for DF-L (with size factor CF and a 1.15 repetitive-member factor, since these span/size checks assume joists spaced ≤24" o.c.), checking bending and live-load deflection only — shear and bearing at supports are not checked here, same as the Beam Sizing tab. Each bay and overhang above is checked independently (bay = simple span, overhang = cantilever from its bearing), and one common size is suggested that satisfies all of them at once — the worst bay or overhang governs. These will not exactly match a specific published AWC/IRC span table (which may use slightly different reference values), so still confirm against the current adopted IRC/AWC span tables and Oregon amendments before use in a drawing set. Also remember: if your load case isn't a plain floor (a deck at 60 psf, for instance), you must change the Dead/Live load fields above — they do not update automatically from context. Sizes checked run 2x6 through 2x14; if nothing that size works, look at an LVL/I-joist on the LVL/I-Joist Calc tab instead.

Footing / Bearing

Service-level (unfactored) loads only — this sizes/checks soil bearing pressure against an allowable value you provide, it does NOT check concrete design (one-way/punching shear, flexure, or reinforcing) or overturning/sliding. Footing self-weight and any soil surcharge above the footing are NOT added automatically — fold them into the load you enter if you want them reflected. Eccentricity is uniaxial (one direction at a time, computed by e=M/P) — a footing with real biaxial eccentricity needs a full two-way check, not this tool. When e exceeds the kern (L/6 or W/6), the soil is assumed to lift off part of the footing and pressure is redistributed as a triangular block over the remaining bearing length — a condition worth avoiding under sustained loads even if the sized/checked qmax still passes; sizing mode rounds the solved dimension UP to the nearest inch, so the actual qmax at that rounded size is always at or slightly under qa, never over. The allowable bearing value is whatever you type in qa — the Site Data (ZIP) tab can hand you a rough regional placeholder as a starting point, but always confirm the real number against the project's actual geotechnical report before finalizing a footing size.

Site Data (ZIP)

Values are coarse 3-digit-ZIP regional estimates, not a site-specific hazard report. Ground snow load in the Cascades/Rockies foothills and the eastern Idaho/Yellowstone corridor is strongly elevation- and fault-proximity-dependent — always confirm snow against the state/county-adopted snow load map (SEAO for Oregon; local jurisdiction maps for WA and ID) and confirm wind/seismic against the ASCE 7 Hazard Tool (asce7hazardtool.online) before finalizing a design. Coverage: Oregon (970–979), Washington (980–986, 988–994), and Idaho (832–838) 3-digit ZIP prefixes. Elevations are regional-default (largest city/town in that prefix) — always enter the actual site elevation above when you know it, since it drives the snow load estimate directly.

Load Path

This traces load paths GEOMETRICALLY — matching analytical member endpoints against each other within a small tolerance — because the current Revit Structural Analytical Model API doesn't expose a direct "what supports this" query (confirmed against Autodesk's own API docs/forums, not assumed). It will read ordinary end-to-end framing correctly but can miss or misjudge unusual conditions: offset connections, transfer members, anything not geometrically coincident at a shared point. Tributary area is a simple nearest-neighbor half-distance estimate per column (like a quick hand sketch), not a true tributary-polygon solve — rougher on irregular or transfer framing, and NOT computed for walls (continuous footings show connectivity status only, no accumulated load). Required footing size uses simple average bearing (P/A, no eccentricity) — it does not read the actual size of the footing family already in your model, and does not check concrete design, overturning, or sliding. Confirm anything this flags against the actual model and a real structural analysis before relying on it.

PDF Compare

Pages align by the page NUMBERS you set above, not by title block or sheet number — if a sheet was inserted or removed mid-set, the two page numbers will drift out of alignment further into the set. Step pages independently on each side to re-sync. On render resolution: a literal 600 DPI render of a full 24"x36"+ sheet is roughly 20,000+ pixels wide — no browser canvas or in-browser pixel diff can hold or process that without crashing the tab. "Maximum" renders at 4000px, which is the highest width this tool can diff at interactively; on a 30"-wide sheet that's about 130 DPI on-screen, and combined with scroll-wheel zoom (up to 6x) gives you well beyond 600 DPI of effective magnification once you're zoomed into a detail — the rendered pixels are just being magnified further, same as zooming into any raster image. For true pixel-level, print-resolution inspection of one specific area, download the current view as PNG and open it in an image viewer at 100%.

Sheet Index

Sheets that don't "Appear In Sheet List" (Matt's proxy for his "Unused" Sheet Collection convention — not confirmed to exactly match) are already excluded by the Revit export and never make it into this index. The export is read-only and never modifies your Revit files. Revision history and hidden items sync to Dropbox through the same connection the Time Tracker app uses — connect Dropbox there once, and this tab picks it up automatically on every device. Until you do, it's local to this browser only.

Rebar Shapes

Bend geometry follows ACI 318 Ch. 25 minimum bend diameters (6db for #3–#8, 8db for #9–#11, 4db for stirrup/tie bends #3–#5) and standard hook extensions — a reasonable field default, not a substitute for checking against the CRSI Manual of Standard Practice or the project's own bar list requirements before fabrication.

PEMB Foundations

A preliminary design for the engineer of record to review, never a stamped design. Reactions are only as good as their transcription. The tab re-computes the PEMB manufacturer's own printed maximum reactions from the basic reactions as a check, and the calc package prints DRAFT until someone ticks the reactions as verified. Combinations follow ASCE 7-16 §2.3/2.4: collateral is dropped from 0.6D/0.9D, seismic Eh is applied ± with the 0.2SDSD vertical term, and in SDC C–F anchors get Ω0 per ACI 17.10.5.3(d). Footing checks reproduce ENERCALC "General Footing": horizontal at the top of the plinth, friction + passive on the footing face, dead-load parts resisting overturning. The results were checked against the two ENERCALC runs in the 26-012 calc (Criteria step). When hairpins or a tie carry the frame thrust, the pad is checked without that horizontal, as in the SE's "W/ hairpins" run. The slab-uplift formula, 0.666 width factor, 0.5 edge reduction and 20' stemwall passive length reproduce the SE's spreadsheet. They are the SE's assumptions, so change them on the Criteria step if he does. MBS frame tables report in-plane H only. By default the longitudinal bracing horizontal is added at braced frame columns, and bracing verticals are taken as already in the basic reactions. Confirm that with the manufacturer on every job. OCR of scanned sets is a draft: amber cells were auto-corrected and red cells were unreadable. Ask the manufacturer for the native PDF, or use the AI-extraction prompt.

How to use the PEMB Foundations tab

New tab (between Footing / Bearing and Section Properties) in tamarack-field-reference.html. It takes you from the PEMB reaction drawings to a preliminary foundation design, a calc package for the SE, and a Revit placement file.

Workflow (4 steps in the tab)

Each step is laid out in outlined, lettered areas (A, B, C…) so you work top to bottom without jumping around. The step buttons show what is still open. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo any change; Esc closes a pop-up.

  1. Project — A · Projects: your jobs, newest first, with Open / download / delete on each row, search, and New / Open file / Save / Save as / Rename / Download across the top. Projects save automatically in this browser. B · Bring in the PEMB reactions: drop the reaction PDF (MBS-format tables from ROI and most MBS manufacturers, and Nucor "Reactions By Load Case" reports read directly; OCR for scans; AI-assisted extraction as a fallback). C · Versions & change history: dated snapshots with notes, and every edit with its own Undo.
  2. Check inputs — three checks across the top (reactions, layout, criteria), each opening its sub-tab.
    • Reactions: the reaction table (headers stay in view) with the PEMB drawing page beside it when the PDF is open — click a column id to jump to its page; the transcription check; the sign-off (the calc package prints DRAFT until it is ticked); load-case mapping.
    • Layout & grids: building and grids (editing a grid moves its columns), columns, door jambs, bracing; tick "I checked the grids…" when done.
    • Criteria: the design-basis check against the PEMB data, then every value that comes from the EOR or the geotech, each marked confirmed or assumed with its source. Marking a value assumed adds a Note to the SE; confirming it closes that note. Method options are under "advanced".
  3. Design — the plan on the left, a tabbed panel on the right, and every column's results below.
    • Plan: scroll to zoom at the cursor, drag to pan, Fit, Zoom to selected; colour by worst check, sliding, anchors or footing type; Layers; hover a footing for its size and worst ratio. Click a footing to review it; shift-click or shift-drag to pick several and change them together. Draw / delete grade beams from the toolbar.
    • Footing tab: the footing type dropdown shows this column's ratio with every type; change the shared type or only this column (it gets its own type); B / L / T with − / + buttons; auto-size; bars. The plinth works the same way (X / Y / height, U-bars, "Size for this base plate"). "Load along the wall" offers dowels into the slab or an along-wall grade beam for braced bays. All checks, the anchor layout and section, the hand calculation and the frame-line reactions (pop-ups) are here too; ‹ › steps through the columns.
    • Types tab: footing and plinth type cards with − / + sizing and auto-size, Consolidate (sizes each column alone and proposes the fewest footing types for the least concrete), and the defaults by column kind.
    • Plan / 3D: the switch in the Foundation header shows a 3D model (footings, plinths, stemwall and wall footing, grade beams, plates, column stubs) — drag to orbit, right-drag or shift-drag to pan, scroll to zoom, 3D / Top / Front / Side / From below views, click anything to open it.
    • Depth: in the Footing tab, "Lower by" drops that one footing below the typical depth (loading dock, grade change); its plinth grows by the same amount so the top of concrete stays put, and the checks use the deeper footing.
    • Walls tab: stemwall and wall-footing sizes with the bearing check, and lowered wall zones (wall + footing step down along part of a wall); "Match columns on this stretch" lowers the column footings there too. The wall and its footing are placed in Revit with the lowered zones.
    • Grade beams tab: the list, the beam editor, and ways to add them.
    • Issues tab: every review flag with its fix one click away (auto-size, own type, dowels into slab, plinth sized for the plate…), Go to, Send to SE, Acknowledge, and the Notes to the SE.
  4. Deliver — A · Before you issue lists what is still open with a Fix link for each; B · Calc package (letter size, prints to PDF; review workbook .xlsx); C · Revit link: Send to Revit saves the design to SE Review\PEMB\<job>\placement.json (the same folder connected on the Home tab); the pyRevit button QA tab → PEMB panel → Place PEMB Foundations lists the jobs there, places everything once (keys FTG/, PL/, GB/ in Comments) and saves placed.json as the baseline. After that the button offers Check model: it reads the model back without changing it, highlights elements changed since placement in orange and saves model-check.json; press Reload here to see each difference (design changed, changed in Revit, both, deleted, extra, duplicate) with Go to, Use Revit value and Mark corrected. When the list is clear, Save as new baseline. Re-place (delete and rebuild) is still there, behind a warning; the ENERCALC method check is at the bottom.

Reviewing the design (added for Cody)

The tab and the calc package now have six review aids:

  1. Frame-line review. Every rigid frame and endwall is labelled on the plan ("RIGID FRAME 2 (MBS 2*)", "ENDWALL 1") and each column is tagged with its id. Tap a frame to see:
  2. its reactions laid out the way the manufacturer prints them, with an MBS-style frame sketch
  3. the manufacturer's printed maximums recomputed for that frame
  4. the design result at each of its columns

The calc package has one page per frame line, or per group of identical "2" lines, with a key plan. 2. Hand calculations. Pick any column and any combination. The tab writes out every number the checks use, with the substituted equation: load build-up case by case, self weight, eccentricity, soil pressure, uplift, overturning, sliding, flexure, shear and anchor bolt forces. The package prints this for the governing column of each footing type. 3. EOR review guide. Page 2 of the package is a six-step checklist with page references: reactions, transcription, basis, governing results, spot check and method. Below it is a one-line governing summary per footing type and per anchor group, plus a sign-off block. 4. Review workbook (.xlsx). - Cody's own "PEMB Footings-master" layout, rebuilt with this job's numbers and live formulas in the same cells. - The ENERCALC sliding-capacity cells are now live formulas (μN + passive). - Also included: an envelope of every check at every column, and every ASD/LRFD combination at every column, with filters. 5. Method validation. - Ten ENERCALC values from his 26-012 runs are reproduced. - The Temple et al. (1991) worked example (49.5 kN) is reproduced exactly. - His spreadsheet's slab value (53.2 kN / 6.0 k) is reproduced. 6. Transcription check.* 32 of the manufacturer's 32 printed maximums are recomputed from the basic reactions and match.

Slab uplift (Temple, Loong & Monforton 1991, Can. J. Civ. Eng. 18:378–387)

The tab uses Cody's version of the equation exactly: Ps = 0.6 Ks^0.2 h^1.4 B^0.56 fr, with his 0.666 width factor and 0.5 edge reduction. Things to know from the paper:

  • Interior footings only. The equation is for interior footings with the slab continuous all round. Applying it to perimeter PEMB columns rests on Cody's edge reduction and width factor, which are his judgement. The paper does not give them.
  • Joints. It is a first-crack load, and the paper notes that construction joints reduce it. Keep slab sawcuts and joints away from the columns.
  • Footing top tension. The paper warns the footing can fail in top tension before the slab does. The tab now checks this ("Flexure top — uplift held by soil/slab"): the net uplift is held down on top of the footing, and the footing is checked as plain concrete.
  • Modulus of rupture. The paper uses fr = 0.6√f'c (MPa), which is 2.75 MPa at 3,000 psi and 2.49 at 2,500 psi. Cody's sheet uses 2.9. The package prints both.
  • Units. Ks is in N/mm³ (0.1 is the paper's average, about 368 pci). The "60" in the English column of Cody's sheet is not used by the formula.

Getting around ENERCALC

Cody only takes the footing sliding resistance (plus the bearing, OT and uplift results) from ENERCALC. The tab now computes those the same way ENERCALC's General Footing does: friction μN plus passive on the footing face, horizontal force applied at the top of the plinth, and dead load counted as resisting.

It was rebuilt with the inputs from the 26-012 calc and matches ENERCALC on:

  • sliding capacity (3.837 / 7.357 / 1.20 k)
  • OT (8.10 / 30.787 and 21.48 / 7.972 k-ft)
  • uplift (6.60 / 3.716 k)
  • bearing (0.920 ksf)
  • flexure (0.8964 / 0.9917 k-ft/ft)

One triangular-pressure case differs by 0.7%. The Method validation page in the calc package shows the side-by-side for Cody. If he still wants ENERCALC as the record, the tab's inputs are the same numbers he would type in.

What I found on Crook (for Cody)

  1. The calc used a different reaction set from the ROI drawings (F1–F3, 03.06.2026). The calc has PDL 1.5 / PWL −11.0 / PEQ −2.3 k. The ROI drawings give Dead 2.1, worst wind uplift −9.4 and Seismic_Long −2.7 k. The Hilti runs used the same older numbers.
  2. Design basis mismatch. ROI designed for 101 mph and 20.3 psf snow. S-001 says 110 mph and 25 psf roof snow.
  3. F2 steel is below the minimum. (5) #4 each way in a 4'-0" square, 12" footing gives 0.25 in²/ft, less than 0.0018bh = 0.259 in²/ft (ACI 7.6.1.1). The calc used (4) #5, which is 0.31 and passes. The schedule and the calc disagree.
  4. F1 (3'-0") bearing is 1.02 under ROI's endwall unbalanced snow (E1UNB 9.6 k at 1-B / 1-C). The calc's endwall run did not include unbalanced snow.
  5. Plinth dowels. A and B plinths are below the 0.005Ag dowel minimum (ACI 16.3.4.1): A needs 1.68 in² and has 1.60; B needs 1.40 and has 1.20. The hooked verticals have about 8" available in a 12" footing against about 9.5" for l_dh. Cody to confirm whether he applies 16.3.4.1 to plinths that are integral with the stemwall.
  6. Hilti seismic combinations. SDC D anchors should carry Ω0 on the seismic combinations (ACI 17.10.5.3(d)). Wind still governs here.
  7. Minor calc cleanups:
  8. Cover says "Seismic Risk Category = D" (should be Risk Cat II, SDC D).
  9. The endwall ENERCALC run is set to ASCE 7-10 combinations.
  10. Hairpin and grade-beam sheets say "grids 1-9" and "grids 2-8".
  11. The building uplift component includes collateral.

Jager (26-004) check: what was added so the tab can engineer it

Jager is a 70' × 150' ROI building (J-114266) with 104 mph wind, 53.9 psf snow and SDC C. Cody resisted the frame thrust with grade-beam ties rather than hairpins. It's now the first example on the Import step. Changes made to engineer it:

  • Grade-beam ties.
  • Enter them on the Layout step, or use one-click "tie every frame" / "tie endwall columns".
  • Each tie is designed for the full factored thrust and for elongation. The U-bars around the anchors are checked as anchor reinforcement.
  • Ties are drawn on the plan, have their own calc-package page and a live-formula workbook sheet, and export to Revit as Structural Framing.
  • Top-and-bottom footing mats. A type can carry "(6) #5 E.W. @ TOP & BOT". Top flexure is then checked as reinforced.
  • Footing edge past the wall. Set per type (e.g. F2 1'-6" past F.O.C.) or per column (corners 1'-4" / 11"). Auto-size also tries centring the footing under the plate.
  • Load point option. Column load at the base-plate centre (actual eccentricity), or at the plinth centroid (concentric, as typed into ENERCALC).
  • Endwall details.
  • Six-column endwalls with different grids at each end.
  • Partial grids, so B/G stop at grid 2 and C/F at grid 8, as in the Revit model.
  • Different corner details at each end.
  • Tension-only X-bracing reversal. "Seismic_LongR" reproduces as the reversed V with H = 0. Snow_Drift and Slide_Snow are recognised, and they are zero.
  • New flags.
  • Seismic RC III against the PEMB's RC II.
  • Ie = 1.0 listed with RC III.
  • Ω0 on anchors in SDC C.
  • The tie/plate couple.
  • Pryout, with a clear explanation.
  • Revit.
  • Type names follow the model: 6'-0" x 6'-0" x 14" DP, 1'-6"WX3'-0"DP, 1'-0" X 1'-0" GRADE BEAM.
  • The script re-uses existing types when their dimensions match.
  • It places the grade beams, and can create the 8" stemwall with a 16" x 8" wall footing.
  • Levels are T.O. FTG and FOUNDATION PLAN.
  • Calc package. Pages that run long now shrink to fit letter size.

What I still need

  • Native PEMB PDFs. Ask ROI and others for the vector PDF, not a scan. It reads exactly.
  • Bracing reactions. Confirm with ROI whether they are included in the basic column reactions. The tab defaults to adding only the longitudinal H at braced frame columns.
  • Revit families and names. Your isolated footing family and parameter names (Width, Length, Foundation Thickness), plinth family (b, h), level and view naming, Revit version, and whether your detail item for anchor bolts should replace the drawn circles.
  • Cody's preferences. Does he keep the slab-uplift formula (0.666 width factor, 0.5 edge reduction), the 20 ft stemwall passive length, and the 16.3.4.1 dowel check?
  • Geotech defaults per jurisdiction (bearing, frost depth, passive, μ). These could come from the Site Data tab.

Other things this could do next

  • Overlay the PEMB anchor bolt plan against the modeled plan in the PDF Compare tab.
  • Push plinth and footing rebar into the Rebar Shapes tab (U-bars, hairpins) for real 3D rebar.
  • Add the typical PEMB details (S-501/S-502) to the Detail Catalog so the pyRevit run also drops the typical sheet.
  • Tie-down / grade-beam option drawn and exported like the hairpins.
  • Batch mode: one PEMB PDF in, calc package and Revit JSON out, saved to the job's Dropbox folder.

Detail Catalog

Getting details OUT of Revit is fully automatic — that part never needs Insert Views from File or any hand-typing. You can still add, edit, or delete a catalog entry right here in the browser too, for anything not worth round-tripping through Revit (a "My Catalog" entry, tagged read-only-safe from the synced ones so a re-sync never touches it). Sync Detail Library is created once (a brand-new Details Library.rvt) and then reused on every later run — it walks a folder of your regular projects, and any project whose file hasn't been saved since the last run is skipped without even opening it, so most runs only touch what actually changed. For a changed project, it pulls in every drafting view that's actually placed on a sheet (its own definition of a "real" detail) AND every legend view outright (legends need no sheet-placement test — they're deliberate by nature), updates an entry in place if you revised it, and keeps both versions side by side if a same-named entry from a different project turns out to have different content. It also tags each detail's Foundation/Floor/Roof/PEMB sheet type from the sheet(s) it's actually placed on — a detail on a "Foundation Details" sheet is a foundation detail even in a PEMB project, checking the sheet name first and falling back to the project name/notes only when no sheet says anything — tagging legends simply "Legend"; use the "Sheet type" filter above to narrow by any of these. It also guesses Element/Material/Connection (Column, HSS, Bearing, and so on) straight from each detail's own view name so you can browse or filter by type — HSS, timber, moment connection, whatever — and remembers which project (and sheet, for a detail) each one was actually pulled from, shown right on the card and inside its own modal as "Pulled from…". Legends have one real Revit limitation: the API can duplicate an existing legend but can't create one from nothing, so both the library and whatever project you're pulling a legend INTO need at least one legend view already sitting in them (even a blank one, made once by hand via View → Legends → Legend) before a legend can sync or place. It writes detail-catalog-export.json itself at the end of every run (no separate step needed), which this tab only ever reads. The older Build Detail Database button still works for a quick refresh if you only changed something in the library by hand. Search is tokenized and ranked like a real search engine — every word you type has to match something (name, view name, element, material, connection, sheet type, tags, source project/sheet, or description), and a hit in the name ranks above one buried only in the description, so a two-or-three-word search narrows in fast without needing an exact phrase. Open a card and click "Place on sheet" to drag a marker onto roughly where it should land — that writes a placement request to detail-catalog-pull.json in the same linked folder, and that card then carries a red "Queued" badge (in the grid and inside its own modal, which lists exactly which project/sheet it's queued for) until "Import Queued Details" clears it. Back in whatever project you're actually working in, running Import Queued Details reads that file, copies the detail's content in from Details Library.rvt, places it on the requested sheet near where you dropped it (Revit centers the viewport there, same as placing any view by hand — expect a small nudge into final position), and trims the request off the queue. Link the folder here the same way as the Rebar Shape Designer's "Link export folder" (File System Access API, Chrome/Edge only); "Re-check now" re-reads the database and your pending requests without waiting for the next page load. For grabbing several details at once, "Add to cart" on any card's modal builds up a shopping cart (shown at the bottom, with an "In cart" badge on each card) — set the project once there and each item defaults to a sheet matching its own sheet type (Foundation to a foundation sheet, Roof to a roof sheet, and so on), editable per item if the guess is wrong or you'd rather send it elsewhere; "Send cart to Revit…" then auto-arranges each sheet's own group of items onto it in a grid and queues them all in one step instead of placing them one at a time. Open a card's modal and use ←/→ (or the arrows beside it) to step through whatever's currently filtered without closing back to the grid first. Standard note blocks work the same way: select the text notes to keep together in Revit, run Save Notes Bundle, give it a title, and it lands in the library tagged "General Notes" — searchable and placeable through the exact same pipeline as any detail. Running it again with the same title updates that bundle instead of making a duplicate.
